cultureAnswer:
Being a part of the Sports Committee at TAPMI, for me, is about creating an environment where sports become more than just competitions, they become a medium for building friendships, leadership, discipline, and a sense of belonging. A strong sports culture is one where every student, regardless of skill level, feels encouraged to participate, improve, and enjoy the experience.
Sports have been an integral part of my journey. As the Sports Captain in school and later the Captain of my university chess team, I learned that leadership extends beyond winning matches. It is about motivating people, creating opportunities, and ensuring that everyone has a platform to perform.
My experience goes beyond participation. As a member of my college's Sports Club, I was actively involved in organizing inter-department tournaments across chess, badminton, cricket, basketball, and volleyball. From managing registrations, team coordination, refreshments, equipment, trophies, medals, and prize distribution to booking venues like badminton courts, I have experienced every aspect of event execution. One of my key learnings was resource optimization, we secured chess boards and digital chess clocks through a sponsorship arrangement where we promoted a local sports store in return. This taught me the importance of building partnerships and finding practical solutions under constraints.
As the university chess team captain, I also conducted chess trials and regular practice sessions throughout the academic year. Beyond selecting the team, my goal was to create a supportive environment where beginners could learn and experienced players could continuously improve. This reinforced my belief that a thriving sports culture is built through consistency, mentorship, and inclusivity.
I also contributed as part of the LEO Club in organizing one of Maharashtra's largest basketball tournaments, where I witnessed the level of planning, coordination, and teamwork required to successfully execute a large-scale sporting event.
At TAPMI, I have already taken a small initiative by creating the "Chess Express" WhatsApp community to connect chess enthusiasts across the campus. We play games online and regularly meet at the Sustainability Block to play, learn from one another, and welcome anyone interested in the game. 
If given the opportunity to be a part of the Sports Committee, I would contribute by organizing well executed events, strengthening participation, encouraging informal sporting communities alongside competitive tournaments, and building meaningful industry partnerships for better resources and sponsorships. More importantly, I want to create an environment where students don't just participate in sports, they look forward to them as one of the most memorable parts of their TAPMI journey.
favoriteMemory:
If I had to choose my favorite sports memory, it wouldn't be a single match or a medal. It would be the feeling that comes with everything surrounding sports, the people, the conversations, the celebrations, the events and even the setbacks.
I still remember the early mornings when my basketball team would gather for practice before the campus had fully woken up. We would train hard, tease each other over missed shots, get scolded by our seniors for not giving our best, and then head for breakfast together. Those breakfasts were filled with laughter, discussions about the game, and plans for the next practice. 
Chess gave me a different kind of joy. Tournaments were intense, Once the pressure was over, everyone would gather around for casual blitz and bullet games. Rivals became friends, spectators became players, and the room was filled with smiles, banter, and endless rematches. Some of my happiest moments were also the simplest ones, playing long games of chess with my sister after a long gap.
Watching sports has been equally memorable. Whether it was cheering from the sidelines as my friends represented the college or celebrating a hard fought victory together, I realized that the emotions of a team are shared by everyone, not just players.
Some of my favorite memories didn't even happen on the field. They happened during late night planning for the event, debating event names, coordinating logistics, arranging sponsorships, and ensuring everything ran smoothly. Seeing weeks of planning transform into a successful event, with players enjoying themselves and the venue buzzing with energy, was incredibly rewarding.

design.whyEvent: I want to join the Event Coordinator Team because it gives me the opportunity to stay connected to sports while creating meaningful experiences for others. I genuinely enjoy the planning, teamwork, and problem-solving that happens behind the scenes of every successful event.

Sports, in some form or another, have always been a massive part of my life. Having played tennis for 15 years, alongside swimming and running, I can confidently say that what you take away from a sport is always more than what you give it.

Beyond keeping you healthy (and sane), sports are hands down one of the best ways to break the ice, meet new people, and bond in a low-stakes environment away from academic stress.

When it comes to building a strong sports culture here, I don't think we need to reinvent anything. The campus already has incredible energy. Events like Speed, Strike, Futsal, and the inter-MAHE tournaments consistently see great participation. My contribution would be in building on that momentum. As the former Sports Head for IPM at TAPMI, I've worked extensively in event coordination and stakeholder management, and more importantly, I've built a strong network across MAHE that I can leverage to increase participation, collaboration, and the overall sporting culture on campus.
favoriteMemory:
My favorite sports memory is from my U-16 district semi-finals match. I had injured my hip in my previous game, so I was already struggling physically going into it. Things looked pretty bleak early on. I was losing 6-2 in an 8-game pro set. But I just dug deep, refused to give up, and slowly clawed my way back point by point until I leveled it at 7-7 to force a tiebreak.
The pressure in the tiebreak was unreal, and to make matters worse, I fell behind 5-2. Needing three straight points just to stay alive, I somehow managed to win five points to take the match. The second the final point landed, my body just gave out and I completely collapsed on the court from full-body cramps.
It stands out as my favorite memory not just because of the comeback, but because of what happened after it. My coach isn't one to hand out praise. But that day was the first and only time he walked up, looked at me, and told me he was proud of the way I played. It's something I'll always remember and often remind myself of when the going gets tough.

TAPMI already has a vibrant sporting culture, and I'd love to contribute towards making events more accessible, and enjoyable for everyone involved. Beyond execution, I enjoy working with people, taking ownership, and creating experiences that bring students together. I believe my prior experience and familiarity with sports administration would allow me to contribute effectively from day one.

cultureAnswer:
Joining Sports Committee for me is not only about being at the forefront of all the events but rather generating a focus on sports for everyone. I would on 2 aspects if given a chance to be in the committee: Participation and Performance. favoriteMemory:
My favorite sports memory has to be Arsenal finally lifting the Premier League trophy this year. For many it was just another year of some team lifting the trophy but for me it was end of a 16-17 years ride of hope, dismay and heartbreak.

Having supported Arsenal since 2010, there were many years when Arsenal were actually predicted to lift the trophy at the beginning of the season but always ended up not winning by the end of it. But that is what made it more special, the team's never die attitude and the zeal to start again from scratch is what kept me going as well. The victory was a reminder that the greatest rewards often come after the longest wait, making the celebration even sweeter. Every setback, every rebuilding season, and every criticism suddenly felt worthwhile. 

People would often think that trophies are achieved over a single season, but this one felt like it was earned over 23 years of hope and unwavering loyalty. That's why this victory will always be my favorite sports memory not because Arsenal won, but because they never stopped believing they could.

favoriteMemory:
The 2024 T20 World Cup final is easily my most unforgettable sports memory—but not just because India won.
It was because of how close we were to losing.
Watching it with my friends, the mood kept shifting between hope and acceptance. After the heartbreak of the 2023 World Cup, none of us were ready to believe fully again. And when it came down to 30 needed off 30 balls, it felt like history was about to repeat itself. Conversations slowed down, expectations dropped—we were already preparing ourselves for another “almost.”
And then, something flipped.
What followed felt less like a match and more like a collective emotional release. Every ball started to matter again. Every moment pulled us back in. The same group that had gone silent was suddenly shouting, calculating, believing.
By the time India crossed the line, it didn’t feel like just a win—it felt like closure. An 11-year wait, all packed into those final moments.
What stayed with me wasn’t just the result, but the journey of emotions within a single game—the doubt, the surrender, the comeback, and finally, the explosion of joy. Watching it with friends made it even more special, because that energy was shared, not experienced alone.
A very close second would be the 2021 Border-Gavaskar Trophy win in Australia. That series redefined resilience for me. It wasn’t the most experienced Indian team, but it was one that refused to back down. It proved that sometimes, belief and grit can outperform pure talent.
And I think that’s why these memories stay—they remind me why I keep going back to sports. Not for certainty, but for moments that feel bigger than logic.

favoriteMemory:
My favorite sports memory is watching the 2022 FIFA World Cup Final live on stream in Kochi. Kerala’s football energy during the World Cup is always off the charts, but that night was something else entirely. Watching Argentina take on France felt less like a football match and more like an absolute cinema that kept everyone glued to the screen. For the first eighty minutes, it looked like a smooth, comfortable victory for Argentina. Messi scored an early penalty, Di Maria finished a brilliant counter-attack, and Argentina was totally in control. But then, complete chaos broke out. In less than two minutes, Mbappe scored twice to bring France back into the game, taking it to extra time. At that point, the tension in the room was unbelievable. Every single person watching was on the edge of their seat, riding every pass, tackle, and shot.

When Messi bundled in another goal in extra time, we thought it was over, only for Mbappe to answer back again with a penalty to make it level. Then came that legendary  save by Emi Martinez which literally saved the dream and forced a penalty shootout.

When Montiel buried the final penalty and Argentina sealed the win, the sheer outburst of emotion was incredible. Being in Kochi, surrounded by die hard fans cheering, screaming, and celebrating Messi finally lifting that trophy after years of waiting, made it an unforgettable moment. It reminded me why we love sports so much the passion, the unpredictable drama, and how a single match can bring thousands of people together in pure excitement.

cultureAnswer:
Being a part of the Sports Committee means creating an environment where sports are not just about competition, but also about community, well-being, and personal growth.

Growing up, sports were a huge part of my life. However, during Classes 11 and 12, the increasing academic pressure made me gradually stop playing. Looking back, I realize that this break affected not just my physical fitness but also my mental health. Sports had unknowingly been my outlet to de-stress, stay active, and feel balanced. Now, as an MBA student in an equally rigorous academic environment, I see even more clearly how important it is to have that space to recharge. Sometimes, an hour on the court can do more for your productivity than another hour behind a laptop.

One thing I have observed at TAPMI is that the sports culture appears to be more centered around male events. While there is great enthusiasm, I believe there is an opportunity to encourage greater participation from women by introducing more inclusive events and creating spaces where everyone feels comfortable joining in, regardless of their skill level.

Personally, I know what it feels like to hesitate because you think you're "not good enough." If selected, I want to challenge those inhibitions, starting with my own, and help build a culture where participation is valued just as much as performance. Winning is important, but sports also teach resilience, teamwork, consistency, and the ability to motivate others through both victories and setbacks.

For me, the Sports Committee is an opportunity to help make sports a space where every student feels welcomed, supported, and encouraged to simply show up and play. I believe joining the Sports Committee is my first step towards having the resources and support to building that committee.
favoriteMemory:
My favorite sports memory is both watching and playing badminton with my mother. When we moved into a new colony in Bangalore, the neighborhood badminton court was always buzzing with people. As the city was embracing its badminton craze, my mother and I decided to join the evening games.

What surprised me most was watching my mother play. Until then, she had only ever been the one dropping me off at badminton coaching, cheering from the sidelines. On the court, she was completely different, confident, competitive, and known for her powerful smashes. I still remember grown men hesitating to return her shots, and watching that filled me with pride.

Beyond the matches themselves, that experience taught me what sports are really about. It wasn't just about winning points, it was about becoming part of a community. As newcomers, we didn't know anyone, but simply showing up every evening helped us build friendships and feel like we belonged. The badminton court became a place where age, profession, and background didn't matter. Everyone was just there to play.

That memory has stayed with me because it showed me that the hardest part is often just taking the first step. Once you show up, you can learn, improve, and become part of something much bigger than the game itself. That's what sports continue to mean to me: connection, confidence, and the courage to keep showing up.

cultureAnswer:
Sports has always been a defining part of who I am. As a state basketball captain for three years and someone who has consistently represented my institutions in competitive sports, I have experienced first-hand how sports develops resilience, leadership and the ability to perform under pressure. At TAPMI, winning the MISS SPEED title and participating in multiple sports has only strengthened my belief that sports has the power to unite people beyond classrooms and batches. 

Over the years, I have also realised that the success of any tournament depends just as much as on the people working behind the scenes as the players on the court. This is what majorly inspires me to be a part of the Sports committee not just to compete but to help create experiences that every student can be proud of. 

If selected, i would like to contribute in 3 key ways : 

First and foremost, i want to make participation in sports more inclusive. A strong sports culture is not built by top athletes ; its built when beginners, casual players and even first-years feel encouraged to participate. Through beginner-friendly practices and open games so students do not feel they need to be 'good enough' for stepping onto the court. 

Second, I want to enhance the visibility and excitement around sports at TAPMI. The sports committee's social media page already captures major moments, but i feel we can make students feel more connected through behind-the-scenes content, training diaries, quick interviews and engaging reels about people saying one liners on their favourite sports and what section they support and making it fun not just for the ones participating but also for the ones watching. When students connect with the people, they naturally become invested in the events. 

Finally, i want to ensure that each event is remembered for its professionalism and energy. I believe every detail contributes to the overall experience. My past leadership roles have taught me how to stay calm, work collaboratively and take ownership when it matters the most. 

For me, joining the sports committee is not just another position of responsibility. It is an opportunity for me to give back to the community that has shaped some of my best college experiences. I want to help create an environment where every student, whether they are on the court or cheering from the sidelines, feel part of something much bigger. That, to me, is what a strong sports culture actually looks like.
favoriteMemory:
One of my favourite sports memories comes from last year's Inter-MAHE basketball tournament during our opening match agains MCON. Although we eventually lost the game, it remains the match that taught me most about resilience. 

We started the game strongly and had good control for most of the first half. However, after halftime, the game became increasingly physical, and the aggressive style of play began to slow us down as a team. In the final quarter, I drove towards the basket with the ball, hoping to convert and important play. An opponent attempted to steal the ball, and when I held my ground, she forced it down with enough impact for me to lose my balance and hit my head on the cement court.

For a few moments, everything around me felt blurry. Players from both teams gathered around as I slowly got back on my feet. I was awarded a technical foul, but I could barely process what had just happened. My teammates and captain kept encouraging me, reminding me to stay focused and trust myself.

As I stepped up to the line, the noise around me was overwhelming. Around fifty people were cheering, shouting, and trying to distract me. In that moment, I blocked out everything except the basket in front of me. Even though we were behind , making that shot felt like my responsibility, not because it would change the result, but because I want to show my team that I wouldn't give up.

I took a deep breath, aimed carefully, and released the ball. The moment it dropped cleanly through the hoop, the crowd around me went silent. It was just one basket, but it meant far more than a point on the scoreboard
 
We lost the match that day, but that shot remains one of the proudest moments of my sporting journey. It reminded me that success in sports is not always measured by victories. Sometimes, it is measured by the courage to get back up, trust yourself under pressure, and give everything you have for your team, even when the odds are against you.

More than anything, I want to be part of the team that creates experiences people look forward to and talk about even after they are over. Whether it's a flagship event or a small initiative, I would love to contribute to making every event run smoothly while ensuring that the participants have an memorable experience. I see the Event Coordinator Team as a place where I can learn and play a meaningful role in shaping campus life at TAPMI.

cultureAnswer:
For me, sports have never been just another extracurricular activity. They've shaped who I am. Some of my earliest memories are of early morning practices, carrying heavy kit bags, travelling for tournaments, celebrating victories with teammates, and learning to accept defeats with grace. Having represented my school at the national level in badminton and swimming, I've experienced firsthand how sports build discipline, resilience, teamwork, and leadership in ways no classroom can.

Being a part of the Sports Committee would mean giving back to something that has given me so much over the years. It's an opportunity to create an environment where everyone, whether they're a national-level athlete or someone picking up a racket for the first time, feels encouraged to participate. I believe the best sporting culture isn't built only by champions; it's built by people who make sports welcoming, enjoyable, and accessible.

One thing I'd love to contribute is increasing participation through fun, low-pressure events alongside competitive tournaments. Activities like mixed doubles, hostel leagues, faculty-versus-students matches, sports relays, and beginner-friendly sessions can encourage more students to step onto the court or field without worrying about their skill level. Healthy competition is important, but so is ensuring people play simply because they enjoy it.

Coming from a sports background, I've also learnt that the smallest things often make the biggest difference—clear communication, fair scheduling, motivated volunteers, and creating an atmosphere where every participant feels valued. As Panther House Captain, I coordinated sports events, mentored juniors, and motivated teams while balancing my own competitions. Those experiences taught me that leadership isn't about being the loudest voice; it's about helping others perform at their best.

Above all, I'd bring positive energy to the committee. Whether it's cheering for a teammate, helping organize events, or encouraging someone who's hesitant to participate, I want to contribute to a culture where sports become a shared campus experience rather than an activity for only a few. If I can help even one student rediscover the joy of playing, I'd consider that a success.
favoriteMemory:
My favorite sports memory has to be the ASISC Regional Badminton Championship final. Even today, whenever I think about it, I can still feel the emotions from that day.

The tournament followed a team format, first singles, doubles, and second singles. We were facing the defending champions, and the stakes were high because the winners would qualify for the national championship.

I played the first singles match, and after the opening matches, everything came down to the final singles. Our doubles team had given their best but had lost under pressure, and suddenly the entire championship rested on one player from our team. Everyone was nervous. The opposition had a huge crowd cheering loudly, trying to create pressure with every point.

As the team captain, I knew I couldn't change the score, but I could influence my teammate's mindset. I kept encouraging her after every rally, reminding her to stay calm, trust her game, and ignore everything happening outside the court. At one point, the opposing supporters became even louder, but instead of getting intimidated, we focused on each point.

The match went into three games. Every rally felt longer than the last. When the final point was won, it didn't feel like just another victory, it felt like a reward for every early morning practice, every difficult training session, and every moment when we chose to believe in each other.

What stayed with me wasn't the medal or the qualification to nationals. It was the realization that leadership isn't always about scoring the winning point. Sometimes it's about giving someone else the confidence to do it.

That match changed the way I looked at sports. It taught me that success is built on trust, encouragement, and teamwork just as much as talent. Even today, whenever I step into a competitive environment, whether it's sports, academics, or organizing events, I carry that lesson with me. Sometimes, the best contribution you can make is helping the person next to you believe they can win.

name: Mahi Palit
achievements:
Sports have always been an integral part of my life. I began training professionally in badminton at the age of 12 under Mr. Arvind Bhat, a former international badminton player and two-time National Champion. Under his guidance, I competed in several state-level tournaments and represented Karnataka at national-level competitions.
During my undergraduate at TAPMI Bengaluru, I represented both TAPMI Bengaluru and MAHE Bengaluru in inter-collegiate and university tournaments. One of my major achievements came in April 2026 when I had the opportunity to captain the MAHE Bengaluru badminton team at BITS Goa Spree 2026, where we emerged as tournament champions.
Apart from badminton, I have represented my school in football tournaments, winning multiple competitions, and have also won inter-house championships in both football and table tennis
cultureAnswer:
Having played multiple sports throughout school and college, I understand the commitment, discipline, and teamwork that sports teach. Representing my school, TAPMI Bengaluru, and MAHE Bengaluru has given me opportunities to travel, compete against talented athletes, and experience how well-organised sporting events create unforgettable memories.

My experience also extends beyond playing. During my internship with the Grand Prix Badminton League, a badminton league featuring the top 64 players ranked in Karnataka, I worked with the operations team where I managed logistics, coordinated with players and management, and handled on-ground responsibilities including scheduling, scoring, registrations, and event execution. This experience taught me how much planning and coordination go into conducting successful sporting events.

As a member of the Sports Committee, I would contribute by:
1. Organising and conducting well-planned tournaments - Creating an inclusive sporting culture where beginners feel just as welcome as experienced players.
2. Encouraging students from all batches to participate through fun leagues, beginner-friendly events, and mixed-team competitions.
3. Promoting fitness by motivating students to make sports a regular part of their lifestyle. Personally, I stay active through badminton and fitness training in the gym.
4. Building a stronger sports community through discussion forums, newsletters highlighting achievements, match previews, post-match analysis, and even student-led commentary teams during major events.

Above all, I want every student at TAPMI to feel that sports are not just for competitive athletes but for anyone looking to stay active, build friendships, and create lasting memories.
favoriteMemory:
If I had to pick one favourite sports memory, it would actually be two moments that mean a lot to me.

The first was when I had just started training professionally in badminton. Every day started at 4:30 AM, when my dad would wake up with me and drive me to the academy. I'd spend two hours there before I rushed off to school. There definitely were days when I struggled to stay awake in class, but those mornings always made me feel like I'd already accomplished something before most people had started their day. One memory that perfectly captures this and that still makes me smile is walking out of the house at 4:30 in the morning for practice while my sister was walking in after a late-night party. We both laughed and I headed to practice while she headed to bed. 
More than the matches or medals, I miss the atmosphere of training - the people, the coach, the drills, everything. Those early mornings taught me discipline, hard work and resilience. Even today, I enjoy waking up early and heading to the gym because that routine has stayed with me.

The second memory is winning BITS Goa Spree 2026 as the captain of the MAHE Bengaluru badminton team. It wasn't just about lifting the trophy, it was about sharing that moment with people who had worked hard, supported each other and celebrated every point together.

cultureAnswer:
For me, I like to observe people in a normal environment, I don't like to stand out immediately. But when it comes to sports, I am a completely different person. My competitive nature comes out while playing sports like Football, Cricket, Badminton etc. (Mainly football though). Something about playing for a team, where each and every one gives their all to win, regardless of how good you are at the sport, is what I like to see. And I also want to see everyone around me with that same level of passion towards sports. Sports are meant for everyone, not just the ones who are good at it. That is the type of sports culture I believe in, and I feel that my values align with the purpose of the Sports Committee as well. favoriteMemory: Ever since i was a kid, I loved watching football, I got into Football because of Lionel Messi in the 2014 World Cup. Seeing his efforts, and seeing his level of play, made me a FC Barcelona and Messi Fan. Although the next year they won the Champions League, since I was still new to football, I didn't appreciate that achievement as much as I should have. But after watching for years and years, in the 2022 World Cup, it felt like Messi's final chance to win for his country. Seeing him overcome his past failures and help his country win the world cup has to be my favorite sporting memory. The way the entire Argentina team, even their coach would give everything on the pitch for Messi, as those players were also his fans during their childhood, it felt like the ending of a Movie, with everything coming full circle. The finals of The World Cup between France and Argentina was the perfect matchup, a team who already won everything and was looking to dominate against a team who had no other option but to win. When the final penalty was scored by Montiel, me and all of my friends were jumping up and down, screaming, hugging random people and celebrating. cultureAnswer:

favoriteMemory:
One moment that has stayed with me forever happened on Independence Day during an inter-school football tournament.

We were up against Greenwood High in the semi-finals. Honestly, we weren't the stronger team. We didn't have a coach, we barely practiced together, and since our school was split into ICSE and CBSE, only a handful of us from the CBSE section made up the football team.

Before the match, our opponents looked confident and well-prepared. They were warming up properly while only three of us were doing the same. As soon as the game started, it felt like they were in complete control. They kept possession almost the entire first half and scored twice. At halftime, the score was 2–0, and most of us had already accepted that we were going to lose. I even noticed my PT teacher standing outside the ground, ready to leave because he thought the match was over.

Then something changed.

I still can't explain it. It felt like a switch flipped inside me. Suddenly, I wasn't thinking about the score or how good the other team looked. I just wanted to fight until the final whistle.

Within the first minute of the second half, I got the ball and scored. I didn't celebrate. I ran into the goal, picked up the ball, and placed it back at the center circle because I knew we weren't done yet.

That goal changed everything.

My teammates came alive. Everyone started believing. A few minutes later, I passed the ball to a teammate, and he scored. It was 2–2.

With about five minutes left, I got the ball again. I dribbled past a couple of defenders and took the shot. To this day, I remember that moment in slow motion—the strike, the silence for a split second, and then the ball hitting the back of the net.

3–2.

We had completed the comeback.

We didn't go on to win the tournament, but that match has stayed with me ever since. It taught me one lesson I'll never forget: never judge a book by its cover. The other team looked bigger, stronger, and far more experienced, but the game wasn't decided by appearances. It was decided by belief, resilience, and refusing to give up.

Whenever I face a difficult situation now, I think back to that match. Sometimes all it takes is one moment, one goal, or one person to change the entire game.

I won 2nd in ASISC athletics - nationals meet - 100m hurdles in 2017

cultureAnswer:
Being a part of the Sports Committee, to me, isn't just another campus responsibility; It feels like an opportunity to contribute to something that has shaped who I am for as long as I can remember. 

I've been a sportswoman all my life, and very few things bring out the same level of excitement in me as stepping onto a track or a court, competing, or even standing on the sidelines cheering for my team. Sports have taught me discipline, resilience, and teamwork in a way that nothing else has. It's also helped to curb the extreme competitive spirit by teaching me how to handle both victory and disappointment with humility and grace. But most importantly, it's given me a community. And to have that sense of belonging is something I would, without a doubt, want every student here to experience. 

I genuinely believe that passion shows through effort. If there's one place where I know I'll always give more than what's expected of me, it's here; not because it feels like a committee role obligation I have to fulfil, but because this is exactly the kind of work I want to be doing. Whether it's being involved in planning tournaments, coordinating logistics, ensuring every participant has a smooth experience, or solving last-minute problems, I know I'd come with nothing but energy because I genuinely care about the outcome of it all. 

As much as I know I am a competitive sportsperson, and more often than not I play to win, I also know this may not be the case for every other person. Sometimes it's just a way to unwind after a hectic day of classes/quizzes/other stressors. Many just want a reason to step onto the field for the first time. As someone who is also deeply interested in event management as well, I'd love to be part of a team that helps cater to all of the types of people I mentioned above, making participation feel welcoming, enjoyable and most importantly accessible to all. The strongest sports cultures aren't only built on medals and championships; but also when students look forward to showing up, supporting one another, and finding joy in being active. 

For me, being a part of the Sports Committee would be more than just an extracurricular commitment but also an opportunity to learn, take accountability and ownership and really understand what goes into creating sporting experiences that people genuinely remember. I want to contribute ideas, take responsibility and be someone the committee can rely on when things get demanding. 

At the end of the day, I don't think my contribution would come from claiming I'll work harder than anyone else. It would come from the fact that this work aligns so closely with who I am. When people talk about things they love, it shows on their face. Sports and athletics have always had that effect on me and I genuinely hope the same enthusiasm translates into creating an environment where more people at TAPMI discover that feeling for themselves.
favoriteMemory:
The memories that have stayed with me the longest, all represent different reasons why I love sports. 

The first is the moment I crossed the finish line in the 100m hurdles finals at the ASISC nationals meet in 2017. I don't remember my competitors; I don't remember the noise around me. All I remember is turning around less than a second after I dove head first across the finish line, and seeing my dad's face, gleaming ear-to-ear with pride. After years of morning sessions, evening sessions, skipped events and parties, sore muscles and injuries, it's cliche to say it, but it all felt worth it in that moment. It made all that sacrifice feel worth it and till date, even with all the other accomplishments I've had over the years, this will still be among my top 3 proudest moments in my life. Having parents who were athletes and sportspeople themselves, they were my official coaches for all of my events; so winning that race meant everything to me and to them. More than this, being able to say I didn't need a professional coach when I had them, was easily my biggest flex :)

Another memory that I'll always cherish is going for IPL match screenings with a room full of people, more often than not, they were my people, supporting the RCB while I sat there with full confidence in my CSK jersey. It's funny how the atmosphere during a close finish can feel even more intense than an exam hall. Every boundary, every wicket, every last-over equation has an entire room reacting in unison. What I love the most isn't just the air of excitement, but the sense of community it creates. Even when people are passionately supporting opposing teams, there's an unspoken respect for the game and for each other. That shared energy is something I've always found incredibly special. 

A friend once told me, that cricket isn't just a sport for us, it's a religion. Something I still believe. 

Another memory I can't go without mentioning isn't one from a particular day, but from every olympic season growing up. I'd watch events until the very last second before leaving for school, and then rush back home hoping not to have missed anything. I will remember sitting completely still during 100m finals, barely blinking, barely breathing until the race was over, and then jumping up in excitement watching athletes like Sha'Carri Richardson dominate the track or watching Sydney McLaughlin redefine what seemed humanly possible. As someone who competed in athletics myself, they weren't just athletes I admired, they were role models who reminded me why I loved the sport and why I wanted to keep pushing myself. 

Looking back, I realise my favourite sports memories have never been only about winning. They've been about the people who celebrated with me, the communities that formed around the game, and the athletes who inspired me to dream a little bigger. That's what sports have always meant to me, and that's why they'll always be such an important part of who I am.

design.whyEvent:
The event coordinator team is where I believe I can contribute the most because it brings together two things that have consistently been a part of my life: sports and event management. 

Over the years, I've realised that what excited me just as much as participating in sports is everything that happens behind the scenes. Planning, coordinating people, anticipating problems before they arise, managing timelines and ensuring an event runs seamlessly are responsibilities I genuinely enjoy taking on. Through my previous college responsibilities, I have had opportunities to organise events and work with divers groups of people, and I've found that I'm best in fast-paced environments where every decision directly impacts the experience of others. 

What draws me to this team is the responsibility that comes with it. A well-executed sporting event doesn't happen because everything goes according to plan. It happens because there's a team that's prepared, adaptable, and willing to do the work no one notices until something goes wrong. That's the kind of role I naturally gravitate towards. I enjoy taking ownership, staying calm under pressure and making sure every participant, volunteer and spectator walks away with a positive experience. 

In the long run, I'm hoping to build a career in event management hopefully with some involvement in the sports industry. While that makes this opportunity personally meaningful, it's also why I know I'll bring more than just commitment to the role. I'll bring genuine curiosity, initiative, and the willingness to constantly improve because this isn't something I'm doing simply to add another position to my resume. It's a space I'm deeply invested in, and that investment reflects in the effort I put into my work. 

I don't see the Event Coordinator Team as something that complements my interests. I see it as a place where my interests, experience, and work ethic can create value for the committee. When people work on something they genuinely care about, they tend to give more than what's expected of them. I know that's exactly the kind of teammate I'd be, someone the committee can rely on, not because they have to, but because I genuinely want to help create sporting events that people remember long after the final whistle.

cultureAnswer:
Being a part of Sports Committee isn't just about organising events and tournaments, to me sports works as a therapy, it states the campus have something besides just academics and competing at the real ground level.
Building networks, teaching teamworks is alot different in theory and practical world. Sports gives us that opportunity to build the real relationships with everyone, get closer to each other and understand the real meaning of management, learn how to tackle stress and how to build and carry a team from scratch. I want to help build a culture where everyone feels welcome—whether they're college-level athletes, weekend warriors, or people who only show up for the free refreshments (we all know they exist🫣). Sports isn't just about physical activities, it can also be the person whose last athletic achievement was finding the shortest route to the mess.
MBA is already a marathon of case studies, presentations, and caffeine. Sports should be the one place where people willingly sweat instead of stress. And if I can convince someone to wake up at 6:30a.m. for a cricket match without offering attendance or placement points, I'd consider that my biggest win.
favoriteMemory: Favourite sports memory that I recall is while playing a cricket match in my hometown. Our team required 25 runs of 12 balls remaining. I was at the other end and when the over began, we hit a 6 on the very first ball. The team bursted into cheers and whistles. The other 5 balls were a nightmare since we lost 4 wickets with and a dot ball in that over. The scene is tensed, filled with pressure and obviously some people would be loosing their money🫣👀. I'm at the strike, the first ball goes dot and everyone started to yell as it was some final of the international tournament. The next ball i hit a 6 (almost would've got caught). Other ball goes dot again and now we need 13 runs of 3 balls. The pressure is intense, but calmed myself somehow and boom the game changed, i hitted 2 back to back sixes with 1 ball to spare. The entire team bursted into celebrations, running towards each other joyfully and celebrating like we have won a cricket world cup that day.

name: ASWIN SAJI
achievements: Won second price in football tournament in higher secondary school.
cultureAnswer:
For me, sport has always been less about competition and more about the break it gives from routine badminton, in particular, has been my go to way to unwind between long study sessions. Being part of the Sports Committee, to me, means creating that same outlet for the rest of the batch: a space where people can step away from case studies and deadlines, even if just for an hour, and come back sharper. It's not just about the players who are already competitive; it's about making sure casual players like myself also feel there's a place for them to show up, play, and stay involved.

I'd want to contribute by helping organize regular, low-pressure badminton sessions and intra-batch tournaments a format that's easy to jump into regardless of skill level, which I think is key to building genuine participation rather than just a committee that runs one big annual event. I'd also focus on consistent communication and scheduling, since a big reason casual players drop off is simply not knowing when courts or slots are available. My goal would be to help make badminton, and sport more broadly, a regular part of campus rhythm at TAPMI, not an occasional distraction something the whole batch looks forward to, not just the ones already good at it.
favoriteMemory:
My favorite sports memory isn't really about a match it's about the man I watched it with. Every time India played, my grandfather would settle into his chair, remote in hand, and call out for me before the toss was even done. Cricket wasn't just entertainment for him; it was a ritual, and somehow, without either of us ever saying it out loud, I had become part of that ritual too.

He was, by every measure, a Sachin Tendulkar fan except you'd never guess it from how he watched him play. Every dot ball, every shot that didn't find the boundary, every dismissal that came a little too early would set him off. "What is he doing," he'd mutter, shaking his head, sometimes getting genuinely worked up over an innings that, in hindsight, was probably still pretty good. As a kid, I used to find it funny how someone could be so annoyed at a player he clearly admired more than anyone else on the field. It took me years to understand that the anger was never really about the shots. It was about how much he wanted Sachin to succeed, every single time, because somewhere along the way, he had stopped just watching him and started expecting greatness from him, the way you do with someone you've quietly grown attached to.

That's why the day of Sachin's retirement is the one I remember most clearly. We watched his farewell speech together, and for the first time, my grandfather wasn't complaining about a single shot. He was quiet. And then, almost without warning, I saw him crying this man who had spent years grumbling at the television, moved to tears watching a career end. I didn't fully understand it then, but I think I do now. My grandfather himself had retired not long before that, and watching Sachin walk off the field for the last time was, in some way, watching a piece of his own life close too. Two men, decades apart in fame but not so far apart in what that moment meant stepping away from something that had defined them for years.

My grandfather passed away five years ago, and cricket has never quite felt the same since. I still catch myself waiting for that call to sit down before the toss, and it never comes. But whenever I watch a match now, some part of that memory comes back his frustration, his quiet pride, and that one moment he let himself cry. It's strange how a sport can hold on to someone for you, long after they're gone. That's what this memory means to me: not the cricket, but the quiet person he was, still very deeply.

name: KAILAS S KURUP
achievements: My only proper achievement in sports was winning third prize in the All-Kerala Under-13 interschool basketball tournament. I guess my luck totally ran out because, after that, my team competed in multiple tournaments across different years but somehow couldn't win any more
cultureAnswer:
Sports has always been an integral part of my life. As someone who struggles to try new things alone, such as participating in group activities or events, basketball was the first sport I joined without any support from parents or friends. From being a shy and hesitant person to trying new things, actively engaging in co-curricular activities and participating in multiple group events, sports helped me overcome these difficulties. The trips we made for each tournament strengthened our team bonding and friendship even further. I believe sports have played a major role in transforming me into a better version of myself. From a person who only played basketball, I now engage in multiple sports like cricket, football, badminton, table tennis, etc.

Being part of the sports committee feels like returning home—doing what I am good at: playing, making friendships, creating bonds, organizing events, and, most importantly, enjoying life. I believe that if you love what you do, you will excel in it, and for me, that is sports.

My contribution will be to proactively engage in all events conducted by our committee, whether it’s speed, strike, futsal, or others. I will also ensure the committee caters to everyone and makes the events a huge success by encouraging student participation and motivating people to step out of their comfort zones and try new activities. Additionally, it is our duty to ensure that all events run by the sports committee are successful and that a spirit of competitiveness is fostered among the students.
favoriteMemory:
My favorite sports memory happened when I was in 12th grade during the All Kerala Inter School Basketball tournament. Whenever I remember this memory, it always brings mixed emotions for me. It is one of those memories that teaches you life lessons.

The tournament date was set, and just one month before it started, our coach got into an accident and broke his arm. We were in our final year of school, and this was our last chance to win a tournament for our school. Our coach was not confident in our team and was thinking of canceling our entry to the tournament. But we went to the management, fought against it, and finally got approval to participate.

We were assigned a junior staff member as our coach was injured, and we went to the tournament without our coach—just 12 students and a junior staff—to a state tournament. To be honest, we were scared because we had fought the entire management to get back in the tournament, and we knew almost all of them were waiting for our failure, which made us fight even harder.

One by one, we won our games and defeated many favorite teams. I still remember on the first day of the tournament when the match sheet was given, nobody knew our school’s name. But by the time we reached the semifinals, the look in their eyes was enough to know that they would never forget our school’s name.

Our journey ended when we lost to the reigning champions of the past 10 years by just 1 point. But I will never forget that tournament. Despite the loss, the hardships we went through and the fights we had to overcome made the entire tournament very special—one to keep in our hearts forever. It was never about the trophy at the end; it was much more than that. I don’t know how to express it in words, but when everyone in your life thinks you’re going to fail, and the feeling when you prove them wrong is something much greater.

Having said that, I am flexible in working in any vertical if any help or need arises.

name: Aman Dwivedi
achievements: I actively participated in sports throughout my academic journey. I represented my school at the district level in cricket and volleyball, won multiple medals in the 100-meter and 200-meter track events, and later secured second place in a chess competition during my bachelor's degree.
cultureAnswer:
Sports have always been a big part of my life. I have grown up playing different sports like football, badminton, cricket, and volleyball, and even today I make sure I play regularly. For me, sports are not just a way to stay fit but also something that helps me clear my mind, stay disciplined, and enjoy spending time with people. No matter how busy life gets, I always find time to be on the field because it is something I genuinely love.
I have had the opportunity to represent my school at the district level in both cricket and volleyball, and I was also the captain of my teams. That experience taught me a lot about leadership, teamwork, and taking responsibility. It showed me that a good leader is not just someone who performs well but someone who brings the best out of the entire team. Along with that, I won multiple medals in the 100m and 200m athletics events during school, and during my bachelor's degree I secured second place in a chess competition. Every sport I have played has taught me something different, and together they have helped shape my personality.
Being a part of the Sports Committee at TAPMI would mean a lot to me because it would give me the chance to contribute to something I truly enjoy. I want sports to be something that every student feels comfortable participating in, whether they play competitively or just want to have fun after classes. I know how much sports can help in building friendships, reducing stress, and creating a sense of belonging on campus.
If I get the opportunity to be a part of the committee, I would like to organize events that encourage maximum participation. Along with competitive tournaments, I would also like to have friendly matches, fun leagues, and activities where anyone can join without feeling intimidated. I would also work with the team to make sure our college teams get the support they need to perform well in competitions.
I believe I can contribute because I genuinely enjoy sports and understand what they can bring to a student's life. I would love to help create a campus where sports are not just events on the calendar but something students actively look forward to throughout the year.
favoriteMemory:
My favourite sports memories are the ones that made me fall in love with the game and taught me what it truly feels like to be a part of it. One of those moments was watching my first live cricket match in a stadium. I was so excited that I actually ran from home because I did not want to miss a single moment. As soon as I entered the stadium, the energy of the crowd, the sound of people cheering, and seeing the players I had admired for years right in front of me was an unforgettable experience. It was one of those moments that made me realize why I loved sports so much.

favoriteMemory:
My favorite sports memory as far as I remember currently is related to cricket as for me like every other Indian cricket is an emotion more than a sport and I deeply enjoy both playing and watching it.

On a personal level, one of my proudest memories was being the runner‑up in my city’s cricket tournament. Standing on that field, battling through pressure, and taking responsibility for my team gave me lessons that no classroom could teach. I learned how to stay calm when the odds were against us, how to motivate teammates when energy was low, and how to accept both victory and defeat with grace. That tournament wasn’t just about a trophy—it was about discovering my own ability to lead, adapt, and perform under pressure.

As a fan, my most cherished memory came after the heartbreak of the 2023 World Cup, when the whole world seemed to criticize India. The narrative was that Indian cricket had lost its edge. The 2024 T20 World Cup final will always be one of my favorite sporting memories. India looked in trouble as South Africa needed just a few runs, but everything changed when Suryakumar Yadav took that incredible catch on the boundary to dismiss David Miller. In that moment, hope returned, and every ball after that felt like history in the making. India completed a thrilling seven-run victory, and the celebrations that followed were unforgettable—players in tears, Virat Kohli and Rohit Sharma embracing, and millions of fans across the country celebrating with pure joy. It was a victory built on belief, teamwork, and resilience, making it one of the most unforgettable memories in Indian cricket.

 I also feel proud when Neeraj Chopra won the men's javelin with a throw of 87.58 m, becoming the first Indian to win an Olympic gold medal in athletics which makes whole India proud and have a stand in athletics around the world.

These memories—both personal and national—mean so much to me because they capture the essence of why I love cricket. It’s a sport that teaches discipline, teamwork, and resilience. It builds strong bonds, creates unforgettable moments, and shows us that setbacks are only steppingstones to greater victories.

design.whyEvent:
For me, joining the Event Coordinator Team is not only about organizing event it also includes creating experiences that people remember. I genuinely enjoy this role of organizing and bringing people together, and I see that sportscom and this role as the perfect way to channel that passion.

I have already experienced the thrill of coordination as an organizing member of a city‑level cricket tournament, where I managed schedules, handled logistics, and motivated teams. That taught me how important planning, adaptability, and teamwork are—skills I can directly apply here.

At TAPMI, I want to contribute by ensuring events run smoothly, encouraging participation from all students, and adding creativity to make each program engaging. More than logistics, I see this as a chance to build bonding, culture, and connections that enrich campus life.

Most importantly, I am dedicated and enthusiastic—I love being part of events, whether it’s planning, playing, or simply enjoying the atmosphere. For me, this role is about creating memories, strengthening community spirit, and growing as a leader.

Apart from sports I have also coordinated charity and social events of NGO, volunteer management in college fest and guest lectures in college.

name: Yugam
achievements: For me, one of the major achievements in sports is becoming the captain of my Inter-House Football team in a high-stakes knockout match when my team captain got injured in the previous match and leading the team to victory when I was in class 10th, further becoming the runners-up of the tournament.
cultureAnswer: To me, the Sports Committee isn't just about handing out sports gear, it’s about stress relief, high energy and bringing people together. As TAPMI’s schedule is intense and anyone who loves pushing limits, sports are the best way to blow off steam and build strong bonds with each other. I have an idea right now by which I would contribute to building a strong sports culture at TAPMI. My idea is of sending a poll in every section asking who plays any type of sports consisting of only two responses in which one can choose only one option between Yes and No (it will be mandatory to choose one of them). Then those students who would have chosen 'No' will be called for participating in a sports event which will be organized in our campus itself. The event will have many games like tug-of-war, table tennis and others. This will create a good impact of sports and the Sports Committee itself that those students who don't play sports are getting opportunity to play.

This is my favorite memory because the match winning team was to get prize money (which was the money paid by the losing team) and my teammates decided that the MOM (Man of the Match) will get half of the money if we win and the MOM is of our team. So, I put my full efforts (which I always put) to win the match, not to win that extra prize money but to win the match which is my ultimate goal and we won that match.

I want this role because I love being on the ground, handling live pressure and solving problems so everyone has a great time playing experience.

name: Dhruv Nair
cultureAnswer: Being part of SportsCom, to me, is the natural end of a three-year build-up. I've been at SPEED every year since I joined TAPMI, and honestly, each year made me want to apply a little more. From the stands, I have noticed things like, how a well-run tournament pulls people in, how the energy of a fest depends on a hundred invisible decisions made by the committee weeks earlier. Being part of the first IPM batch has also shaped how I think about contributing to a place. There was no template ahead of us when we joined the first year, no seniors in the same programme and a lot of what we needed we had to figure out or build ourselves. That's given me a real appreciation for people who take on the invisible work of making things run, and a comfort with pitching in wherever the gaps are, without waiting to be told. My main objective will be try to use the things that worked the best for the last 3 years , as thats what was most memorable for me through Speed. I'm applying not because I'm the most qualified sportsperson in the room, but because I've spent three SPEEDs quietly wanting to be on the other side of the field. I think that's a decent reason to show up ready to work.
favoriteMemory: My most memorable/ favorite sports memory relates to my favorite sport that’s Football. So the setting is 2022 world Cup finals, its Argentina Vs France. That I would say is most invigorating match that I have ever had watched, it had everything it had total domination followed by a comeback and of course followed by eventual victory, yes I was a Argentina supporter. I still remember I had a Pre-Board the next day in a subject that I had failed the last pre-board, but I didn’t care because I was witnessing history being made, I was seeing my goat (Messi) achieve a dream of his that he made us believe in. It was just pure emotions even in the end because I remember shouting after Gonzalo’s pen and was in tears because the team had actually done it.

design.whyEvent: Because the coordinator role is where the actual work of an event lives, and that's the part I want to be in. Anyone can enjoy a well-run tournament — very few people see what it took to get there. including all the times the fixtures needed to be changed due to class clashes, all the times the speed SPOC's needed to reminded to be there on time. I'm also drawn to it because it's a role that rewards being useful over being impressive. You don't need to be the best athlete or the loudest voice for once ,you need to be reliable, calm when something goes sideways, and willing to get things done and that matches how I work.
